lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on excellence and exposure
lead.head: Give luck a bigger target
body: Remembering a night in 1988, when Tracy Chapman filled in for Stevie Wonder with an acoustic guitar, brought a phrase to Amit Varma’s mind: the surface area of serendipity.
Luck, the hosts argued, is not pure chance. You can widen the area it can hit.
Varma credited the idea to Jason Roberts and gave it a formula: luck equals passionate doing multiplied by effective telling. In his own alliteration, excellence and exposure. {039-C01}
Chapman had both, he said: thousands of hours of craft behind songs like *Fast Car*, and the luck of being there. One without the other would have come to nothing.

Ajay Shah, as an economist, saw a trade-off. A Jimi Hendrix who practises only in the bathroom has a problem. So does the modern schmoozer, one of the “content-free hustlers” who “actually know nothing”.
## Craft before contracts
In India, Shah argued, the first-order problem is the craft. Many young people he meets want the reward settled before the work begins.
“People want a locked in, visible, clear reciprocity that give me this big lollipop, and then I will put my 50,000 hours,” he said. “And that’s not how life works.” {039-C04}
He pointed to Linus Torvalds, who wrote the Linux kernel with no salary, prize or fame on offer. Greatness, Shah said, takes way more than the popular 10,000 hours.
Varma was careful to add that individuals are not to blame. Generations of scarcity, he said, built a goal-directed culture with little room for anything higher.

There is a better loop, he said, borrowing a line from the show’s crew member Nomsita: she is happy when she does things well, and does things well when she is happy. Its mirror is the vicious cycle of the entitled, in whom mediocrity and entitlement feed each other. {039-C06}
## Out of the house

Exposure comes harder to both men. Varma, a self-described classic introvert, has never marketed the show. Yet the show found its crew the day he happened to go to a Starbucks in Versova and a man he knew only online said hello.

Shah, also a natural introvert, admits that meeting new people is hard. He has learned to do it anyway, and to connect others across disciplines, judging them by their ideas rather than their degrees.
Varma widened the idea. Reading, watching films and making things also enlarge the surface, he said: exposure runs from the world to you as well. {039-C02}
## Less envy, more signal

Shah closed with networks. If ideas passed between people without loss, six degrees of separation would let a musician play for one person and go back to the bathroom, “because then you’re done, then Putin knows”.
“There is transmission loss, and every pipe has limited bandwidth,” he said. Only long-built trust lets a few sentences land with full force. {039-C11}
The fix, Shah said, is cultural. With less envy, resentment and competitiveness, ideas would travel through elite networks with less loss, and everyone would need fewer conferences.
Modern India’s elite culture is still being forged, Shah said, and “the culture is made up out of a million behaviors”. So each of us can help to make it.

second.label: Work and reward
second.head: Lollipop first? No deal
second.deck: Ajay Shah says young Indians want the reward before they put in the years
body: Ajay Shah meets lots of young people, and he sees a pattern. They want a contract, pay and promises before they commit years of effort to anything. {039-C04}

Linus Torvalds, he said, decided as a teenager to write a Linux kernel. Nobody offered him a salary, a job, a prize, fame or glory. Shah, who told that larger story in the show’s Unix episode, is “depressed and disappointed” at how little of such work happens in India. {039-R05}
Demanding a direct link between effort and outcome, he argued, is the path to weakness and mediocrity. His advice was simpler: “Do try. Because what’s the point of living if you don’t?”

quote.text: There is a lack of the inner fire and the devotion and the ability to stay hungry

second.caption: the lollipop before the work

third.head: No lectures, see the blog
body: Early in his career, Ajay Shah was drawn into a good circuit of Indian economics conferences, and he is grateful to those who invited him. As the economics community declined, he said, many of those conferences stopped working, so he grew choosier.

For years he also accepted guest lectures, because teaching works so badly in India. Then he built outlets that run without him: the Leap Blog, which he co-edits, this show, an XKDR YouTube channel, a flow of working papers and a fortnightly column. {039-R18}
Now he declines most speaking and teaching invitations. “I’ve done my responsibility to the universe,” he said. “I’ve built all these things, I point people to them.” {039-S06}
Anything more, he said, “would be a high opportunity cost”.
third.caption: rationing his own exposure

sections.label: The opening
sections.head: The perils of the quick study
sections.caption: his biggest mistake
body: The hosts opened by asking each other an unexpected question. Ajay Shah’s, to Amit Varma, was: what is the biggest mistake of your life?
Varma chose a broad one: he did not work hard enough. He was lost in grand plans, he said, and built none of the processes and habits he now teaches his writing students. {039-S02}

Behind it lay what he called a meta mistake. He came to self-reflection too late. “I think most of us don’t do any self reflection and it’s tragic,” he said. Take five minutes every day to think honestly about yourself, he argued, and you would be amazed at what you see. {#fiveminutes}
## Verbs, not adjectives
Varma does not like the person he was twenty years ago. He was arrogant, he said, because he could study in one hour what took others ten.
He tied it to a study discussed in an earlier episode. Children praised for being smart grew entitled and stopped working hard; those praised for effort kept trying.
“In writing I often say that focus on verbs, don’t focus on adjectives,” he said. “So in a very different context, focus on verbs, focus on doing, focus on working.” {039-C03}
Could he have avoided the mistake? No, he said: he had to live and change before he could even see the option.
~ Shah replied with a saying: “Youth is wasted on the young.” Varma finished it: “and wisdom is wasted on the old.” {039-J12}

quote.text: I just didn’t work hard. I was always floating in my head, lost in daydreams, thinking of grand plans

sections.label: Chapter one
sections.head: Out of the bathroom, Jimi
sections.caption: excellence times exposure
body: Amit Varma calls the two halves of luck excellence and exposure, and believes both need to be got right. Tracy Chapman, he said, spent thousands and thousands of hours becoming good, but she also needed the exposure. {039-C01}

Ajay Shah, as an economist, immediately saw a trade-off. Being “just Jimi Hendrix practicing guitar only in the bathroom”, he said, is a problem. So are the “content-free hustlers who are just trying to go out and schmooze”. {039-J04}
Everyone, he said, should ask where they stand, and whether to push one side up or down a little.
## Beyond 10,000 hours
In India, Shah argued, the primal problem is the first half: people are not committing enough to the craft, the knowledge, the doing.

Nor is the famous 10,000 hours enough. That much practice might get you to play *Für Elise* reasonably well, he said, but creating something new is another level of intensity. Linus Torvalds, Ken Thompson, Chapman, Hendrix and Jimmy Page gave entire lives to their work. {039-C05}
Luck still plays its part. Shah quoted a song: “I don’t know why fortune smiles on some and lets the rest go free.” You don’t control it, he said: “You’ve just got to be zen about it.” {039-J16}
~ The other half of the formula, Shah recalled, was his father’s daily practice at CMIE. That story is on page 3.

quote.text: Actually, glory and greatness is not 10,000 hours, it is way more than that.

sections.label: Chapter two
sections.head: Round and round, up or down
sections.caption: virtuous and vicious cycles
body: Amit Varma wanted one thing clear: the hosts are not blaming individuals. After long years of scarcity, he said, it is natural for a culture to become goal-directed: get into IIT, do an IIM, become a vice-president at Citibank.
A newsletter he wrote on the day of recording was sparked by a line from Nomsita, of the show’s crew: “I am happy when I am doing things well, and I do things well when I’m happy.”

Work done for its own sake, he said, gives joy, and joy drives you deeper. The vicious cycle belongs to the entitled: denied validation, they turn bitter; given it, they decide they never needed to work. {039-C06}
## “I have arrived”
Ajay Shah agreed. The most dangerous thing about being an IITian, he said, is “the sense that I have arrived”, which lets people stop trying for years.
His way out came from Richard Stallman: “a good programmer will never starve.” A day job, Shah said, need not be your whole life. {039-J15}

Nothing gets done quickly, Shah stressed. Of youngsters who want three months on an open-source project to show GitHub on a résumé, he said: “I just want to kick them out of the office that nothing works like that.” {039-J03}
~ The economy of a modern India allows such lives, Shah said. It is the culture that has not caught up.

quote.text: It’s a vicious cycle where the mediocrity and the entitlement perpetuate each other.

sections.label: Chapter three
sections.head: Mavens, meet the connectors
sections.caption: mavens and connectors
body: Amit Varma calls himself a classic introvert. He has never marketed this show or *The Seen and the Unseen*, believing a good product is the best marketing. “Like Sartre says, hell is other people,” he said. {039-J17}

In Malcolm Gladwell’s *The Tipping Point*, mavens go deep into something, while connectors go out and link people. Varma counts himself a maven, and wondered whether, through an act of intentionality, he should try to be more of a connector. {039-C08}
Ajay Shah admitted that he too struggles to get to know new people. All of us look brusque and prickly from a distance, he said; once you get going, there are no strangers.
## Ideas, not degrees
Mentors such as Rakesh Mohan, Suman Bery, Vijay Kelkar and Montek brought Shah into India’s economics community when he was new. He tries to do the same, in two ways of his own.
First, he ignores credentials. “I don’t care about Harvard, MIT, IIT, whatever,” he said. What matters is whether a person is asking interesting questions. {039-C09}
Second, he connects people across economics, finance, public policy, software and statistics, people who would never bump into each other at a conference by chance.
~ Earlier that day Shah had taught Varma a word for this: superconnector. Varma said Shah was one.

quote.text: I don’t have the personality to be a connector, to just turn to a stranger at a conference

sections.label: The reccos
sections.head: One film every three years
sections.caption: the golden age of cinema
body: Asked for a recommendation, Amit Varma said he felt inspired, and chose a film that inspired him at seventeen or eighteen: Peter Weir’s *Dead Poets Society*. Just thinking of it, especially its last scene, made him well up. Its message, in his words: seize the day, *carpe diem*.
Ajay Shah drew a blank. “You cover up for me and produce a second recommendation,” he said.
## A golden age

Varma chose Justine Triet’s *Anatomy of a Fall*, winner of the Palme d’Or at Cannes. It made him realise, he said, that this is a golden age of cinema, whatever Marvel and Bollywood suggest. {039-R11}

Any film, by telling a story, edits reality and simplifies the world, he said. Great art also honours its complexity. *Anatomy of a Fall*, a courtroom drama and a domestic drama, is literally about that trade-off. {039-C13}
Then he turned to his co-host. If you watch one film every three years, “like Ajay Shah here”, he said, change, because great art can help you understand yourself. {039-J08}
~ His parting advice to Shah was to watch as many films as he can and skip boring conferences, because “all these economists say the same damn things”.

quote.text: great art is great because it acknowledges the complexity of the world.

side.boxText: Amit Varma credits the luck surface area to a gentleman named Jason Roberts. The definition he read, from an essay linked in the show notes: luck is the action you take towards your passion multiplied by the number of people you effectively tell. {039-C01}

contQuote.text: It’s about exposure, not just of you to the world, but of the world to you. Read more, watch more, think about ideas, all of that.

p3.title: Lucky breaks
p3.deck: Four times chance found someone ready for it, and what each one teaches

stories.start: In 1988, there was a concert called the Nelson Mandela Tribute concert.
stories.end: she made it more likely that good things would happen to her.
stories.caption: Tracy Chapman’s lucky night
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the night Stevie Wonder lost a disc
stories.head: A missing disc and a fast car
body: *Fast Car* has been Amit Varma’s all-time favourite song since it came out in the late 1980s, though he and Tracy Chapman, he said, have nothing in common. When she sang it at the Grammys recently, he remembered how the song became famous. {039-R01}

In 1988, massive crowds gathered for the Nelson Mandela Tribute Concert. Stevie Wonder was due on with his band. As the equipment was unpacked, he found that a computer disc with programmed music he needed was not there.
Wonder said he absolutely could not perform without it. According to one report, Varma said, he went off in tears. He was not throwing a tantrum, Varma added; he was really upset.

The organisers had an empty slot and tens of thousands of people waiting. Chapman, who had played a set earlier to a smaller crowd, happened to be around with only an acoustic guitar. They asked her to fill in. {039-S03}
She sang a couple of songs, one of them *Fast Car*, and it went “madly viral, as much as something could go viral in the days before the internet”.
Before the concert, her album had sold about 200,000 copies. {#sales} In the two weeks after it, it sold two million.

~ Just being there, Varma said, does not mean good things happen to you. Chapman had spent thousands and thousands of hours becoming good, and without great songs nobody would have asked her. But being there made good things more likely.
stories.why: Chance paid off only because both halves were in place: the craft, and the being there. Luck, in the formula Varma read out, is passionate doing multiplied by effective telling. {039-C01}
stories.postscript: Without that turn of events, Varma said, he might never have heard the song.

stories.caption: a hello at Starbucks
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the hello that found the show its crew
stories.head: Hi, you’re Amit, right?
body: A few months earlier, Amit Varma was sitting in a Starbucks in Versova when a bearded man a couple of tables away said: “Hi, you’re Amit, right?” It was Vaibhav, who runs Chalchitra Talks. They had worked together online but never met. {#hello}
Vaibhav, Varma said, is a natural connector who takes the initiative. As they parted, Varma realised the show might soon need a new crew, so he took his number.
When the time came, he messaged Vaibhav, who sent him Nomsita’s number. The crew that followed, Varma said, is a blessing.
~ He need not have gone out that day. “I’m a classic introvert,” he said. “I don’t go out much, I don’t do stuff.” {039-S05}
stories.why: A small rise in exposure can change a life in ways nobody plans. Varma was wary of making it advice, though: just because he got lucky, he said, does not mean you will. {#wary}

stories.caption: his father’s daily rounds
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on how his father built CMIE
stories.head: The man who kept walking
body: In 1976, Ajay Shah’s father started CMIE, the first project of its kind he had ever done. He went out of his way to leave the house every day, meet people and campaign for it. {039-S04}
There was no email and there were no smartphones. Shah’s father set up meetings anyway, a group of conversations every day where he got to tell people what he was trying to do. {#smartphones}

~ His reasoning was common sense, Shah said. If you are building an important new organisation, you have to go out and talk to the whole world about it, sell people on the dream and get more and more of them to join hands.
~ He had a Sanskrit proverb for it, which he often told his son.

quote.text: Charati Charato Bhaga, which translates to good things happen to those who walk.

stories.start: The luckiest thing that ever happened to me was that I got to be
stories.end: And it was just dumb luck that happened to be there at that
stories.caption: the luckiest thing that happened to him
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the luckiest thing that ever happened to him
stories.head: A walk-on part in a war
body: Ajay Shah finished his PhD in the United States in 1993. India’s reforms had begun in 1991, and he had a gut instinct that a dramatic time lay ahead.

He could have stayed in America. He weighed it with a lyric: “Would you exchange a walk on part in a war for a lead role in a cage?” {039-J11} “It would be more interesting. It would be more challenging. I had no idea what was going to happen,” he said. He relocated to India. {039-S01}
Around that time, a team including R.H. Patil, Ravi Narayan and Chitra Ramakrishna was building the National Stock Exchange. Shah got to be a bit player in it.
~ He calls it one of the most interesting and exciting times of his life. “I couldn’t ask for better,” he said.
stories.why: Shah calls it dumb luck. But the luck found him because he chose the riskier, more interesting place to be: the episode’s theme in a single life decision, made without knowing what would come of it.

quiz.q: What did Stevie Wonder find missing before the 1988 Nelson Mandela Tribute Concert?
quiz.a: A computer disc with programmed music he needed, so Tracy Chapman filled in.

quiz.q: In Jason Roberts’s formula as Varma read it, luck equals passionate doing multiplied by what?
quiz.a: Effective telling: the number of people you effectively communicate your passion to.

quiz.q: What Sanskrit proverb did Ajay Shah’s father quote while building CMIE, and what does it mean?
quiz.a: Charati Charato Bhaga: good things happen to those who walk.

quiz.q: According to Ajay Shah, how is the quality of a conference panel related to fame?
quiz.a: It is inversely proportional to the fame of the people on it.

quiz.q: Which two types from Malcolm Gladwell’s *The Tipping Point* did Amit Varma weigh himself against?
quiz.a: The maven, who goes deep, and the connector, who links people together.

quiz.q: Where was Amit Varma when a chance hello eventually found the show its new crew?
quiz.a: At a Starbucks in Versova, where Vaibhav of Chalchitra Talks said hello.
